summary:
Guyana criminalises consensual same-sex conduct under the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, retained in force after independence. Section 351 punishes an act of gross indecency between men, in public or private, as a misdemeanour carrying up to two years' imprisonment. Section 353 punishes buggery as a felony carrying life imprisonment, with related provisions covering attempted buggery. Some compilations cite the same offences as sections 352 to 354. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions structure police encounters with lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people and sustain public stigma.

A constitutional savings clause bars judicial review of laws inherited at independence. The clause prevents courts from invalidating the inherited sexual offences even where they conflict with human rights guarantees, so repeal depends on Parliament rather than litigation.

The cross-dressing offence in section 153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice on 13 November 2018 in McEwan, Clarke, Fraser, Persaud and SASOD v Attorney General, as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. The challenge followed the 2009 arrests of transgender women under the 1893 provision and three nights' detention, a 2010 Supreme Court filing with SASOD, a 2013 Chief Justice ruling permitting cross-dressing unless for an "improper purpose", and affirmance by the Court of Appeal.

Guyana provides no procedure for legal gender recognition. No sourced provision addresses transgender-specific identity documents, airport screening, facilities, custody or gender-affirming care.

Police use residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses against LGBT people. SASOD's Joel Simpson documented men in "compromising positions" threatened with arrest to extract bribes, same-sex couples harassed at seawalls and parks, and complainants who face secondary discrimination at stations and give "watered down" accounts. Loitering and vagancy clauses remain usable after the 2018 ruling, chiefly against sex workers.

Street violence and justice-system failure are documented together. Petronella Trotman, a trans woman, was stabbed in Georgetown in January 2017; on 2 March 2017 magistrate Dylon Bess refused her entry to the Georgetown Magistrates Court because she was not "dressed like a man" and her case against her attacker was dismissed. At the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 191st session in November 2024, a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition on violence against migrant women, sex workers and transgender women; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action, with 69 documented cases of violence against trans women recorded for 2018 to 2022, a raw count the source gives without a population denominator.

No hate-crime legislation covering gender identity or sexual orientation exists. Simpson was beaten by six men in Georgetown on 16 June 2019 after harassment at a nightclub, filed a police complaint and called for such legislation; the Ministry of Social Protection condemned the attack while affirming acceptance.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions do not exist in Guyana. Adoption, foster care and guardianship are not barred: the U.S. Department of State reports that LGBTQ people are not disqualified, and in December 2015 the Director of Guyana's Childcare and Protection Agency stated the agency does not discriminate and encouraged LGBTQ people to become adoptive parents.

Decriminalisation carries political backing. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, including the ruling party, supported it, and President Irfaan Ali promised in September 2025 to decriminalise with SASOD. An October 2022 poll of 1,070 respondents found 72.4% accepting or tolerating LGBTQ people, up from 34.5% in 2013, with reported hatred down to 12% from 25%.
tangentialFactors:
Guyana is the only country in South America and the only mainland country in the Americas where homosexual acts remain illegal, and one of five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct. The regional comparison runs the other way on court-led reform: Belize in 2016 and Trinidad and Tobago in 2018 struck down analogous bans, routes unavailable in Guyana because of the savings clause.

Constitutional protection on sexual orientation was unanimously approved in December 2000 but denied presidential assent before the March 2001 elections after religious opposition; a 2003 reintroduction was withdrawn without progress. Legislative reform has been announced and stalled repeatedly since, including a 2012 national-debate announcement, a 2013 parliamentary commission that received submissions in 2014, a 2017 referendum proposal later described as a misunderstanding and opposed by SASOD, and a May 2019 SASOD call for the Law Reform Commission to remove archaic clauses.

Public attitudes are recorded as shifting. The 2013 CADRES survey found 24% "hate" homosexuals, 38% tolerant and 25% accepting, with 53% supporting criminalisation; LAPOP's AmericasBarometer score rose from 7.2 in 2010 to 20.6 in 2017 on a 0-100 scale against an Americas average of 26.8; a 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance and 13 percentage points less hostility than in 2013.

Pride mobilisation has proceeded with state tolerance. The first parade took place on 2 June 2018 in Georgetown without violent incident despite a demand from a ministers' fellowship for a ban, followed by a 2019 festival with a 1 June parade of 200 under police protection during which participants faced shouted insults, postponements in 2020 and 2021 for COVID-19, and the largest Georgetown event in June 2022.

A July 2019 Court of Appeal reduction of Clive Knights' 57-year murder sentence for the 2012 killing of Bert Whyte to 30 years for manslaughter after a claim of "unwanted homosexual advances" illustrates how sexual-orientation framing enters sentencing.
localsOnly:
Article 149 of Guyana's revised Constitution guarantees equality and non-discrimination. In July 2019 the Government told the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women that it recognised its responsibility to remove legal gaps preventing discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and affirmed that every individual has the right to live free from violence, abuse and discrimination regardless of those characteristics.

SASOD cooperates with the Guyana Police Force hierarchy to retrain officers to respond professionally to LGBTQ complaints and service access, and works with health professionals, the University of Guyana and nursing schools across the country on knowledge of LGBTQ people. Cabinet approved a sexual and reproductive health policy inclusive of sexual orientation.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, no hate-crime statute covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no access to same-sex marriage or civil unions. Adoption, foster care and guardianship remain legally available. Discrimination and violence at the hands of law enforcement, religious leaders and others are described as widespread, leading most LGBTQ people to conceal their orientation, with gay men commonly labelled "anti-men". Hate crimes often go unreported.
outOfScopeNotes:
Section numbering for the sexual-offence provisions is unresolved across sources: Wikipedia cites sections 351 and 353 of the Criminal Law (Offences) Act 1893, while Outright's overview cites sections 352 to 354 for the same offences. Both describe the same conduct and penalties.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules, identity-document markers, airport or border screening, bathroom or facility access, detention or custody placement, or access to gender-affirming care for visitors. The absence of such provisions is stated where the sources speak to it; beyond that, these areas are not sourced here.

The figure of 69 documented cases of violence against trans women for 2018 to 2022 is a raw count with no population denominator and no comparison to Guyana's general violence rate, so it indicates documented pattern and official concern rather than a measurable rate of risk.

The frequency of prosecutions under sections 351 and 353 is described as rare by two sources but no case counts are given. Whether the constitutional savings clause would bar a challenge to a future repealing statute is not addressed in the inventory.
